storm.summary_layperson: A cluster of showers and storms is sitting about 32 miles to the west-northwest and drifting only slowly toward the cove, with a wide arrival window sometime between roughly 12:45 PM and 5:15 PM.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The air-water temperature gap (4.7°F) is only enough for a weak marine layer, below the threshold where the cove's protective Sound effect reliably kicks in.
storm.detail_html:
Radar (KOKX) shows a cluster of cells 32–36 miles WNW of the cove, topping out at 40–42 dBZ — real convection, not clutter, but distant and slow-moving. Current instability is low (CAPE 190 J/kg, 0–6km shear 12.3 kt), which is a weak setup for organized severe weather. The OKX forecast discussion flags a better chance of isolated afternoon storms after 2 PM, with modeled instability (MUCAPE) rising to 500–1,000 J/kg, mainly north and west of NYC — HRRR's own extended outlook agrees, showing CAPE climbing from ~130 J/kg now toward a 3–8 PM average near 360 J/kg (peak 620 J/kg) and shear building toward ~20 kt.

The cove's usual protective mechanism — a cool, stable layer of air sitting over Long Island Sound that can choke incoming convection — is only weakly in play today. Water is 74°F against inland air near 79°F, a 4.7°F gap that classifies as a weak marine layer. That falls short of the ~10°F gap the pipeline requires to call the Sound effect "active," so the cove gets only modest, not strong, risk reduction relative to inland towns.

Most likely outcome: any storm that organizes inland this afternoon will be somewhat slower to reach and somewhat weaker by the time it crosses the Sound, but this is not a case where the cove should expect to sit under a bubble untouched while surrounding towns get hammered — the delta is too small for that. Inland Westchester and the area north/west of NYC carry the higher risk of an isolated afternoon cell.

The radar-tracked cells are moving very slowly (closing speed ~5 kt) and radar could not measure their true motion vector directly (no coherent echo to track between scans), so the arrival estimate below leans on modeled HRRR steering rather than measured storm motion — treat the timing as a wide window, not a fixed point.

What would change this call: any cell strengthening past 45 dBZ within 25 miles while still closing, a Severe Thunderstorm or Tornado Watch/Warning issued for Fairfield/Westchester counties, or the marine layer strengthening (water-air gap widening) which would sharpen the protective effect. Also watch the AFD's afternoon punch-through scenario — if MUCAPE reaches the upper end of its 500–1,000 J/kg range while the marine layer stays weak, that favors an earlier, more intact arrival rather than a late, weakened one.

arrival.blurb: Radar-detected cell 32 mi WNW, but with no measurable radar motion the timing relies on model-estimated (HRRR) steering, so lean on the wide window, not the point estimate.

wind.tactics_blurb: A sea-breeze day reinforced by a light onshore background flow — expect a steady SSW breeze building through 6–8 kt by early afternoon. Pressure is fairly uniform across the course; start mid-line and play the oscillations once the breeze matures after 1 PM.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a sea-breeze day reinforced by the background gradient (internally "A+") rather than a pure thermal day. The air-water temperature gap is 4.7°F at 9:35 AM and rising fast as morning patchy fog clears and the sun comes out — the sea-breeze gate (≥5°F) is expected to clear right around the start of this window. The background gradient itself has a light onshore (southerly) component per the NWS forecast (S at 1–9 mph), which reinforces rather than opposes the thermal circulation — the classic A+ setup, stronger and steadier than a pure thermal day would be on its own.

Riverside YC is already reading SSW 5 kt gusting 7.3 kt at 9:35 AM, and the western-LIS station ensemble is 70% southerly with the median already at SSW 200° — the sea breeze is filling in early and faster than HRRR's raw model output has caught up to. HRRR's f01–f06 hourly forecast for this morning shows light (1–3 kt), oscillating E/SE/ESE directions that diverge over 160° from the current observed SSW flow — a clear case of the model lagging the real sea-breeze veer described in the direction-maturation framework. This table overrides the raw HRRR direction with the observed/maturing sea-breeze axis (SSW) for the full window rather than quoting the stale model numbers; treat this as a manually-applied maturation correction.

Speed-wise, HRRR's own extended outlook (aggregate for the 3–8 PM stretch) shows wind averaging 6.2 kt with a ceiling of 8.0 kt, which lines up well with the mid-window peak of 8 kt used here — good cross-check even though that outlook carries no per-hour direction breakdown.

Shift character: expect a steadily-veering, persistent right shift through 11 AM–1 PM as the sea breeze ramps up (classic early-SB behavior, not yet oscillating), transitioning to a mature, tactically-playable oscillation of roughly ±10° once established after about 1 PM. With SSW–SW flow, cove geography is fairly uniform across the course — maybe marginally stronger near the mouth and east shore — so there's no strong lane to bank on; start mid-line and play the shifts rather than committing hard to one side. Wind stays in the 6–8 kt range all window — good one-design dinghy racing, not powered-up, and no postponement risk at these speeds. Sunset isn't until 8:10 PM, so nothing in this window threatens a collapse.

data_caveats: Wind direction for 11:00–17:00 overrides raw HRRR (which showed light, oscillating E/SE/ESE readings) with the observed sea-breeze axis (SSW) already established at RYC and the western-LIS ensemble — HRRR's frozen 8 AM run had not yet resolved the sea breeze.

HRRR only provides per-hour wind detail through 2 PM EDT (f01–f06); the 15:00–17:00 rows use the established sea-breeze direction plus HRRR's aggregate extended-outlook speed envelope (mean 6.2 kt, range 3.1–8.0 kt) rather than per-hour model output.
Storm arrival timing is low-confidence: radar could not measure the cell's motion (no trackable echo between scans), so the ETA uses modeled HRRR steering rather than radar-tracked motion.
Buoy 44040 / WLIS reading is 77–80 minutes old — sea-breeze depth signal over open water is somewhat stale.
